lesson_title: Ransomware: the Payment and the Cash-out

metadata.reading_assignment: FBI, Affidavit in Support of an Application for a Seizure Warrant, Case 3:21-mj-70945-LB (7 June 2021): paras. 16-22 and 24-33

lectures.title: Ransomware: the Payment and the Cash-out - lesson synthesis
Ransomware: the Payment and the Cash-out - assigned reading

questions.question_stem: A ransomware analyst and a theft analyst both start work. What is unusual about where the ransomware trace begins?
questions.correct_answer: The victim knows the address it was told to pay, so the trace starts from a known, dated payment and not a guess.
incorrect_answers: The criminals post the ransom address on a public leak site, so any analyst can find the first hop unaided.
Ransom payments go through a ledger the victim controls, so the victim supplies each hop after the first.
Ransomware gangs reuse a single address for every victim, so the start of the trace is the same each time.
questions.explanation: Colonial told the FBI the address it was told to pay, and the ledger is public. The trace starts at a known, dated payment; what follows is judged hop by hop.
questions.lesson_block: Ransom: a payment you can watch from the start

specific_source.anchor: Ransom: a payment you can watch from the start

questions.question_stem: A DFIR firm negotiates and pays a ransom, buying the coins at an exchange. Which side of the payment does that exchange's record cover?
questions.correct_answer: The victim's side: who bought the coins and sent them, often from a hosted wallet.
incorrect_answers: The criminal's side: who controls the ransom address and will spend from it later on.
The split: how much of the ransom went to the developer and how much to the affiliate.
The cash-out: which service the criminal used afterward to turn the coins into money.
questions.explanation: The victim side of a ransom runs through a regulated exchange; the criminal side starts at the ransom address. The note, the portal and the exchange each leave something to ask for.
questions.lesson_block: A note leads to a portal, a price, an address

specific_source.anchor: A note leads to a portal, a price, an address

questions.question_stem: Colonial paid about 75 BTC on 8 May 2021, and the ransom moved four times in two days. What does that pace mean for the analyst's note?
questions.correct_answer: The trace starts from a dated payment within a day, so each hop gets its own date to record.
incorrect_answers: Ransoms sit for weeks, so early hops say little and the trace should begin at the cash-out.
The shutdown time fixes when the address was made, so each hop can be dated from the note.
Fast movement shows the criminals cashed out at once, so the trace has reached a service by hop two.
questions.explanation: The timeline slide dates the note, the payment and each hop. The ransom moved the same day it was paid, but nothing in the timeline says it reached a service.
questions.lesson_block: Colonial: shut down at dawn, paid the next day

specific_source.anchor: Colonial: shut down at dawn, paid the next day

questions.question_stem: In the Colonial trace, hop 1 sends 75.0003 BTC to one address and 0.00001693 BTC to another. What does the lesson's annotated trace write for it?
questions.correct_answer: Change undetermined: make no call, give no confidence, and follow both outputs as leads.
incorrect_answers: The larger output is change, since the payer keeps most of the value; follow only the other.
The tiny output is change, since dust amounts are always change; follow the larger.
Probably the larger output is change, rated Low until a later hop confirms it, so follow that.
questions.explanation: Nothing in that single transaction shows which output is change. 'Change undetermined' is a correct answer with no confidence word, and both outputs stay leads.
questions.lesson_block: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

specific_source.anchor: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

questions.question_stem: Two branches of the Colonial ransom arrive at one address, and the lesson rates 'one holder' Moderate, not High. Why?
questions.correct_answer: It rests on ledger clues alone and fails if that address belongs to a service holding many customers' coins.
incorrect_answers: High needs five hops in a row, and only three hops of the trace support the call in this particular case.
An explorer's unverified label is the only thing supporting it, so the call is Low and not Moderate.
The amounts are not round, so no heuristic applies and the call is only a guess about who the holder is.
questions.explanation: Same-transaction clues stop at Moderate on the course scale. High needs a different kind of evidence, and a shared address could be a service's.
questions.lesson_block: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

specific_source.anchor: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

questions.question_stem: At hop 5 an explorer groups the spending address with 23 other addresses as 'one wallet' without showing why. How does the lesson rate that?
questions.correct_answer: Low: it is an explorer's label, and checking the co-spending yourself would make it your own judgment.
incorrect_answers: Moderate: explorers apply the co-spend rule, so their label counts as a trace the analyst did personally.
High: the explorer is a source separate from the affidavit, so the two lines are independent.
No rating: a label from an explorer is not a finding, so the note should leave it out entirely.
questions.explanation: An unverified explorer label is Low. Checking the transactions raises it only as far as same-ledger evidence goes; High needs something off-chain.
questions.lesson_block: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

specific_source.anchor: Each hop gets a heuristic and a confidence

questions.question_stem: A student's trace ends at an address holding about 69.6 BTC that has not moved. What should the student's note say?
questions.correct_answer: The trace ends at a holding address, not a service, as of the date checked, with leads listed.
incorrect_answers: The trace ends at an exchange, because a large balance that stays still shows a service is holding it.
The trace cannot be written up, because a trace counts only once it has reached a named service.
The ransom was seized, because coins that stop moving have been taken out of the criminals' hands.
questions.explanation: A trace ends at the first service or where the money stops. 'Has not moved' is true only as of a date, so the date goes in the note, with leads such as the 11.2496 BTC output.
questions.lesson_block: This trace stopped at a wallet, not a service

specific_source.anchor: This trace stopped at a wallet, not a service

questions.question_stem: Hop 3's smaller output is 11.2496 of 75 BTC, about 15%. A colleague calls it the developer's cut for certain. What is the best response?
questions.correct_answer: It fits a developer's share, but no rate is stated for this ransom size, so amount alone is Low.
incorrect_answers: Agree, because in any split the smaller output goes to the developer and the larger to the affiliate.
Reject it, because a ransomware-as-a-service split never appears on the blockchain at all.
Rate it Moderate, since the two outputs add to the ransom, which shows the split was deliberate.
questions.explanation: The developer's share fell as ransoms grew (reportedly 25% under $500k, 10% above $5M), but no rate is given for about $4.3M. Amount alone is Low.
questions.lesson_block: Developer and affiliate split it on-chain

specific_source.anchor: Developer and affiliate split it on-chain

questions.question_stem: The affiliate's shares of the Colonial and Brenntag ransoms went to one wallet. What can an analyst take from that?
questions.correct_answer: Shares go to separate wallets, so a shared affiliate wallet suggests one affiliate hit both victims.
incorrect_answers: The developer attacked both victims, since the developer receives each ransom before any affiliate.
Both victims paid through one exchange, since affiliates can only be paid from an exchange account.
Both victims were given one ransom address, since a group issues a single address to every victim.
questions.explanation: Elliptic reports the affiliate's shares of both ransoms reaching one wallet, 'suggesting' a single party. It is a lead on who, not a proof.
questions.lesson_block: Developer and affiliate split it on-chain

specific_source.anchor: Developer and affiliate split it on-chain

questions.question_stem: Why does the lesson tell the analyst to name the first service a ransom reaches?
questions.correct_answer: That service keeps customer records, which are off-chain evidence that can support a stronger one.
incorrect_answers: That service must freeze the coins, so naming it lets the analyst stop the ransom moving any further.
That service converts the coins to cash, so the trace continues only through a bank account.
Services publish their customers' addresses, so naming one lets the analyst read an identity.
questions.explanation: The on-chain trace stops at the first service and the off-chain records begin. Freezing coins is legal process, which is out of scope.
questions.lesson_block: A ransom cashes out at a service

specific_source.anchor: A ransom cashes out at a service

questions.question_stem: Hydra sold goods to its users, yet the lesson lists it among ransomware cash-outs. Why?
questions.correct_answer: A market is both a shop and a route: about $8 million of ransomware proceeds passed through it.
incorrect_answers: It was an exchange under another name, so each sale on it was really a ransomware payment, not goods.
It sold nothing at all, so its customers were all victims paying a ransom demand to the site itself.
It was run by DarkSide's developer, so affiliates were paid from its accounts before cashing out.
questions.explanation: The slide lists darknet markets, with about $8 million through Hydra, among ransomware cash-outs, and calls a market both a shop and a route for money.
questions.lesson_block: A darknet market is a shop and a cash-out

specific_source.anchor: A darknet market is a shop and a cash-out

questions.question_stem: A colleague says coins paid on a darknet market are untraceable, so the trace ends when a ransom reaches one. Which reply fits the lesson?
questions.correct_answer: Users often wrongly believe so; a market is a service, so the trace reaches it, and its vendors cash out onward.
incorrect_answers: That is right, since darknet markets accept only coins whose ledger hides both the sender and the amount paid.
That is right for payments but wrong for withdrawals, since a market always knows who its customers are.
That is wrong, because markets must register and publish a list of their vendors, so every payment is attributed.
questions.explanation: A darknet market is a service like an exchange. Silk Road took Bitcoin only, a public ledger, and a trace that reaches a market has reached a service.
questions.lesson_block: A darknet market is a shop and a cash-out

specific_source.anchor: A darknet market is a shop and a cash-out

questions.question_stem: In the Silk Road filing, which findings came from the ledger and which needed the market's own records?
questions.correct_answer: Round amounts and timing are ledger patterns; the market's own database showed they were not staff or vendor withdrawals.
incorrect_answers: Everything is ledger evidence, so any analyst could conclude from the pattern alone that the coins were stolen.
None of it is ledger evidence, because the round amounts were reported to officers by the market's own operator.
The theft was shown by the ledger, while the round amounts and the timing came from the market's own database.
questions.explanation: The ledger patterns raised the question, and the market's database, an off-chain record, settled it.
questions.lesson_block: Silk Road: stolen coins left in round amounts

specific_source.anchor: Silk Road: stolen coins left in round amounts

questions.question_stem: Silk Road's stolen coins were gathered at address 1HQ3, and Colonial's at an address that has not moved. How do the two traces end?
questions.correct_answer: Both are holding addresses, but 1HQ3 also sent 101 BTC to an exchange, so that trace reached a service.
incorrect_answers: Both reach an exchange, since any address that gathers coins into one place is a service's deposit address.
Colonial's reached an exchange and 1HQ3 did not, since 1HQ3 held all of its coins until a seizure.
Neither is a holding address, since both sent value on in the end and so were ordinary wallets.
questions.explanation: 1HQ3 sent 101 BTC to BTC-e in 2015 while 69,370 BTC stayed there; Colonial's trace ended at the wallet. Each note says which, and as of when.
questions.lesson_block: Silk Road: stolen coins left in round amounts

specific_source.anchor: Silk Road: stolen coins left in round amounts

questions.question_stem: A case agent hands the analyst only a copy of the ransom note. What should the analyst ask for first?
questions.correct_answer: The ransom address and payment transaction, since the trace starts there and the note gives a Tor site.
incorrect_answers: The criminals' Tor site address, since the portal's page shows each later hop of the ransom for the analyst.
The exchange's customer service desk, since the exchange can tell the analyst where the coins went next.
The developer's wallet address, since the developer's share is the first output of every ransom that is paid.
questions.explanation: The victim holds what the chain does not: the address, the transaction, the portal chat and who bought the coins. These are leads, a different kind of evidence from the ledger.
questions.lesson_block: The portal and chat are leads; ask for them

specific_source.anchor: The portal and chat are leads; ask for them

questions.question_stem: A briefing line reads 'ransomware took $820 million in 2025, down 8%'. What must go with the figure?
questions.correct_answer: The source and its as-of date, noting the total is likely to rise as more payments are attributed.
incorrect_answers: Nothing more, because an on-chain total counts every payment exactly and cannot change once published.
A note that the median payment fell, because fewer victims paying means each payment is smaller.
The names of the victims counted, because a figure cannot be used unless every payment can be listed.
questions.explanation: The total 'is likely to approach or exceed $900 million' as attribution catches up, and fewer victims paid but the median payment rose. A figure needs its source and date.
questions.lesson_block: Fewer victims pay, but each pays more

specific_source.anchor: Fewer victims pay, but each pays more

questions.question_stem: The Colonial affidavit prints every address with its first characters hidden. What does that mean for an analyst checking the trace?
questions.correct_answer: The ledger still shows each full address, and the printed amounts and dates let you find every transfer.
incorrect_answers: The hidden characters keep the transfers private, so only the investigators' own records can confirm them.
Each address must be rebuilt from its last characters, so the trace cannot be checked against the ledger.
The masking also hides the addresses on the ledger, so the transfers stay out of view until they are released.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading masks the start of each address in the document, but it describes the blockchain as a public ledger visible to everyone and prints the amounts and dates in full. The masking is in the filing, not on the chain, so the transfers can still be found and checked.

questions.question_stem: After following the Colonial ransom through every hop, what does the public ledger still not tell the analyst?
questions.correct_answer: Who holds the private key that moved the coins out of each address.
incorrect_answers: Which addresses received the coins and how much each one received.
The dates on which the coins moved from one address to the next.
Whether the coins left the final address or are still held there.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading describes the ledger as recording every address, transaction and balance, open to anyone. It also says only the holder of an address's private key can move coins out of it, and the ledger does not name that holder. The trace therefore runs address to address and stops short of identifying anyone.

questions.question_stem: The affidavit uses an explorer to list each transfer and also to say many addresses sit 'in one wallet'. How should an analyst treat the two?
questions.correct_answer: The listed transfers are ledger records; the wallet grouping is the explorer's own inference.
incorrect_answers: Both are ledger records, since an explorer only displays what the blockchain already stores.
The wallet grouping is a ledger record; the listed transfers are the explorer's own estimates.
Both are the explorer's inferences, since an explorer adds its own judgment to each result.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading defines an explorer as software that arranges blockchain data for search, and it reads each hop's amounts and dates that way. Its statement that 23 or more addresses were collected in one wallet is the explorer's grouping, and the filing does not show the transactions behind it.

questions.question_stem: At hop 4 an address sends a round 63.7 BTC to a new address and a small amount back to itself. Which output does the analyst follow?
questions.correct_answer: The round 63.7 BTC, because the small amount sent back to the payer is change.
incorrect_answers: The small amount, as coins sent back to the payer show where the owner saves.
Both outputs equally, because a single transaction never shows which one is change.
Neither output, because coins sent back to the payer show the trail has been broken.
questions.explanation: The assigned reading records hop 4 as about 0.05 BTC sent back to the paying address and a round 63.7 BTC sent on, and the trace continues with the 63.7. Coins returned to the payer are change by the plainest clue, so the other output is the payment to follow; the lesson rates that call Moderate.
